# Sirach 46 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** Sirach 46 | **Date:** 2026-03-17 | **Total Disagreements:** 17

---

## Disagreement 1 — 46:1, "mighty in war" vs. "a warrior without peer"

**EMET:** "Joshua son of Nun was mighty in war"
**LOGOS:** "Joshua son of Nun was mighty in war"
**PNEUMA:** "Joshua son of Nun was a warrior without peer"
**Issue:** Greek dunatos en polemō = mighty in war. EMET/LOGOS agree literally; PNEUMA adds "without peer" which is not in the text.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS: "mighty in war."

---

## Disagreement 2 — 46:1, "successor of Moses in prophesying" vs. "in the prophetic office"

**EMET:** "successor of Moses in prophesying"
**LOGOS:** "successor of Moses in the prophetic office"
**PNEUMA:** "Moses' successor in the prophetic role"
**Issue:** Greek diadochos Mōuseōs en profēteiais = successor of Moses in prophecies. "In prophesying" (EMET) is more literal; "in the prophetic office" (LOGOS) is more formal.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "in the prophetic office" as the more dignified formulation.

---

## Disagreement 3 — 46:1, "his elect" vs. "his people" vs. "God's chosen people"

**EMET:** "a great salvation for his elect"
**LOGOS:** "a great salvation for his people"
**PNEUMA:** "a great salvation for God's chosen people"
**Issue:** Greek eklogē = election, chosen ones. "His elect" (EMET) is literal; "his people" (LOGOS) is broader; PNEUMA expands.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "his people" — the reference is to Israel broadly, not a subset.

---

## Disagreement 4 — 46:2, "stretched out his hand" vs. "lifted up his hand"

**EMET:** "when he stretched out his hand"
**LOGOS:** "when he lifted up his hand"
**PNEUMA:** "when he raised his hand"
**Issue:** Greek ekteinas cheira = stretching out the hand. "Stretched out" (EMET) is most literal; "lifted up" (LOGOS) implies a different gesture.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "lifted up his hand" — in context it refers to the gesture of wielding a sword, which involves raising.

---

## Disagreement 5 — 46:2, "wielded the sword" vs. "brandished his sword"

**EMET:** "wielded the sword against the cities"
**LOGOS:** "brandished his sword against the cities"
**PNEUMA:** "swung his sword against city after city"
**Issue:** Greek en rhomphaia = with the sword. "Wielded" (EMET) implies use; "brandished" (LOGOS) implies display; PNEUMA's "swung" is more active.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "brandished his sword" — the gesture described is dramatic, suited to the hymn.

---

## Disagreement 6 — 46:4, "one day became as two days"

**EMET:** "one day became as two days"
**LOGOS:** "one day became as long as two"
**PNEUMA:** "one day stretched to the length of two"
**Issue:** Greek kai egenēthē hēmera mia hōs duo = and one day was as two. EMET is most literal; LOGOS adds "long" for clarity; PNEUMA paraphrases.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows LOGOS: "one day became as long as two."

---

## Disagreement 7 — 46:5, "hailstones of mighty power" vs. "hailstones of overpowering force"

**EMET:** "hailstones of mighty power"
**LOGOS:** "hailstones of overpowering force"
**PNEUMA:** "a storm of mighty hailstones"
**Issue:** Greek chalaza en dunamei ischyos = hail in the power of strength. "Overpowering force" (LOGOS) is stronger; "mighty power" (EMET) is more literal.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "hailstones of overpowering force" (LOGOS) — the doubled power word in the Greek warrants a strong English rendering.

---

## Disagreement 8 — 46:6, "his armament" vs. "his full armor"

**EMET:** "that the nations might know his armament"
**LOGOS:** "that the nations might know his full armor"
**PNEUMA:** "The nations learned what his armor was"
**Issue:** Greek ta hopla autou = his arms/armor. LOGOS "full armor" is interpretive expansion; EMET "armament" is more literal.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "armament" — the word encompasses both weapons and armor.

---

## Disagreement 9 — 46:7, "work of mercy" vs. "deed of loyal love" vs. "faithful loyalty"

**EMET:** "he performed a work of mercy"
**LOGOS:** "he performed a deed of loyal love"
**PNEUMA:** "he and Caleb son of Jephunneh had shown faithful loyalty"
**Issue:** Greek ergon eleous = work of mercy/lovingkindness. "Loyal love" (LOGOS) imports the Hebrew hesed concept; "mercy" (EMET) is the standard Greek rendering. "Faithful loyalty" (SOPHIA composite) bridges both.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "a work of faithful loyalty" — combining the sense of EMET and LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 10 — 46:7, "silencing the evil murmuring" vs. "putting an end to their wicked murmuring"

**EMET:** "silencing the evil murmuring"
**LOGOS:** "putting an end to their wicked murmuring"
**PNEUMA:** "silencing their wicked grumbling"
**Issue:** Greek katapauein gonggusmon ponēron = causing the evil murmuring to cease. EMET "silencing" is vivid; LOGOS "putting an end to" is more prosaic.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "silencing their wicked murmuring" (EMET/PNEUMA hybrid).

---

## Disagreement 11 — 46:9, "high places of the land" vs. "hill country of the land"

**EMET:** "he went up to the high places of the land"
**LOGOS:** "he went up to the hill country of the land"
**PNEUMA:** "he climbed into the hill country"
**Issue:** Greek ta hupsēla gēs = the heights of the land. This refers to the hill country of Hebron (Josh. 14:12). "Hill country" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) is geographically precise; "high places" (EMET) could be misread as cultic high places.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "hill country of the land" to avoid the cultic connotation.

---

## Disagreement 12 — 46:11, "play the harlot" vs. "turn to idolatry"

**EMET:** "whose hearts did not play the harlot"
**LOGOS:** "whose hearts did not turn to idolatry"
**PNEUMA:** "who never gave their hearts to idols"
**Issue:** Greek ou porneusantes = not having committed fornication. The metaphor of spiritual adultery/harlotry for idolatry is consistent throughout Hebrew scriptures. EMET preserves the metaphor; LOGOS/PNEUMA interpret it.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "did not play the harlot" — the metaphor is deliberate biblical idiom and should stand.

---

## Disagreement 13 — 46:12, "bones revive" vs. "bones sprout anew"

**EMET:** "May their bones revive from where they lie"
**LOGOS:** "May their bones sprout anew from where they lie"
**PNEUMA:** "May their bones sprout new life from where they lie"
**Issue:** Greek anatolēsai = to rise up, sprout (like a plant). "Sprout" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) captures the botanical metaphor; "revive" (EMET) loses it.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "May their bones sprout anew from where they lie" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 14 — 46:15, "attested as a true prophet" vs. "known as a true prophet"

**EMET:** "he was known as a true prophet"
**LOGOS:** "he was attested as a prophet"
**PNEUMA:** "His faithfulness proved him a true prophet"
**Issue:** Greek epistos = faithful, trustworthy, attested. "Known as" (EMET) is too weak; "attested as" (LOGOS) captures the public verification aspect.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "attested as a true prophet" (LOGOS + EMET "true").

---

## Disagreement 15 — 46:16, "when enemies hemmed him in" vs. "when enemies pressed him in"

**EMET:** "when enemies hemmed him in on every side"
**LOGOS:** "when enemies pressed him in on every side"
**PNEUMA:** "When enemies surrounded him on every side"
**Issue:** Greek ekklisantōn autou = pressing upon/surrounding him. "Surrounded" (PNEUMA) is most vivid; "hemmed in" (EMET) is idiomatic.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA adopts "when enemies pressed him in on every side" (LOGOS).

---

## Disagreement 16 — 46:19, "eternal sleep" vs. "eternal rest"

**EMET:** "Before the time of his eternal sleep"
**LOGOS:** "Before the time of his eternal sleep"
**PNEUMA:** "Just before his eternal rest"
**Issue:** Greek aiōniou koimēseōs = of eternal sleep. EMET/LOGOS agree; PNEUMA simplifies. "Eternal sleep" is the proper euphemism for death here.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA follows EMET/LOGOS: "eternal sleep."

---

## Disagreement 17 — 46:20, "fallen asleep" vs. "died"

**EMET:** "even after he had fallen asleep he prophesied"
**LOGOS:** "even after he had fallen asleep he prophesied"
**PNEUMA:** "even after he had fallen asleep, he prophesied"
**Issue:** All three agents preserve the euphemism "fallen asleep" for death. This must stand — the text is specific that Samuel's ghost spoke (1 Sam. 28), and Ben Sira affirms this as genuine prophecy. All agents agree.
**Resolution:** SOPHIA retains "fallen asleep" — unanimous.

---

*Total disagreements logged: 17*
